clue.text: Conversational gap filler often used by Doctor What's his-name

parts.note: 'you know' is a filler phrase dropped into speech while thinking
the Doctor of the long-running BBC science-fiction series Doctor Who

explanation.surface: A famous TV time traveller habitually pads his talk while forgetting someone's name.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Who is a long-running British TV series; the hero is simply 'the Doctor'. The definition is a stand-in for a name one avoids saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are evasive substitutes used for a person whose name is forgotten or not to be spoken.

clue.text: A key batsman

explanation.surface: A batsman described as crucial to the team.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool that opens locks or tins is one sense; in cricket the two batters who begin an innings are its other sense.

clue.text: Stand guard in hollow beneath castle

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece placed beneath another comes after it

parts.note: the keep is the main tower of a castle
a cave is a hollow in rock

explanation.surface: A sentry posted in a hollow below a castle wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep cave' is old British schoolboy slang for keeping a lookout (cave is Latin for 'beware').
explanation.definitionFit: The schoolboy idiom means acting as lookout for others, warning of approaching teachers.

clue.text: Honours are likely

explanation.surface: Awards or decorations are probably coming someone's way.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games honours (ace, king, queen and so on) are literally printed on playing cards; as an idiom the phrase means probable.

clue.text: When warm, it may be friendly or hostile

definitions.text: When warm, it may be friendly or hostile

parts.words: When warm, it may be friendly or hostile
parts.note: a greeting described as warm is cordial, but a 'warm' reception can also be an ironic way to describe being met with fury

explanation.surface: Musing on how a heated reception can go either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A reception given to arrivals; a warm one is cordial, though ironically a warm one can be angry.

clue.text: Examination, or, rather, a lesson, all very superficial

indicators.note: superficial means only on the surface, so take just the top letter of each of these words

explanation.surface: A teacher grumbling that a test, or a lesson, was shallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all very superficial' takes the first letter of 'or', 'rather', 'a' and 'lesson'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoken test, as in a viva or language exam, is an examination given by word of mouth.

clue.text: List made out but wrongly distributed

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone made out a list but handed things out incorrectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' signals an anagram of LIST MADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer who gives out cards incorrectly has dealt them wrongly, the past tense of a botched deal.

clue.text: Footwork for fencers?

parts.note: fencers use blades and nimble feet, but here the footwork is a Scottish dance stepped over crossed blades

explanation.surface: Asking about the nimble steps practised in fencing.
explanation.definitionFit: A Highland display dance performed over crossed blades laid on the floor, so literally footwork involving weapons.

clue.text: Soldiers have to contend with formal inspection

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to vie is to compete or contend

explanation.surface: Troops must cope with a parade-ground inspection.
explanation.definitionFit: A military parade for inspection by a senior officer or monarch is an official examination of troops.

clue.text: Wrong set in control in base

indicators.note: one piece set in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: a pedal is a foot-operated control

indicators.note: wrong means not right, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Complaining that the incorrect group was put in charge at headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' makes EST, and 'in' is the container signal; the second 'in' is only a link. 'base' is the definition, not a hint at headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth supporting a statue or column is its base or foundation.

clue.text: A firm swimmer out east, I am used to strain

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: out means removed, so the letter is taken away

parts.note: Leander, of Greek myth, swam the Hellespont nightly to meet Hero
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A company swimmer heading off east, used to exertion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes E (east) from LEANDER to leave LANDER. The definition speaks as the object itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A perforated kitchen bowl used to drain pasta or vegetables, so it is a tool for straining.

clue.text: Two hundred square metres of ground

parts.note: an are is a metric unit of a hundred square metres
a is the symbol for the are, another hundred square metres

explanation.surface: A small plot of land measured in metres.
explanation.walkthrough: The are is a metric land unit of 100 square metres; its symbol is a, so the unit plus its symbol make two hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: A tract or stretch of land is a region of ground.

clue.text: Copier provided an issue man resolved

indicators.note: resolved read as re-solved, broken down and worked out afresh, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A problem settled by a man, with a photocopier nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' signals an anagram of AN ISSUE MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A scribe or secretary who writes from dictation or copies manuscripts is a copier.

clue.text: Turn up and revive workman

parts.note: to come to is to regain consciousness, to revive
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A labourer appears and comes round after fainting.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive or become available, as a letter reaching someone, is to turn up.

clue.text: Float made in part from tyre and hose

parts.note: the tread is the gripping part of a tyre
to hose a garden is to water it

explanation.surface: Something buoyant made from a bit of tyre and a hosepipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying upright in water by moving the legs keeps a swimmer afloat without progress.

clue.text: Pupil in time needs support in maths

indicators.note: one piece in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: an age is a period of time
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates
a bra is a supportive undergarment

explanation.surface: A schoolchild, given time, needs help with maths homework.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'maths', with 'in' a link: the answer is a branch of mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of mathematics using symbols for unknown quantities is an example of maths.

clue.text: Peripatetic an expert in disorder

indicators.note: one piece in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: gout is a disorder of the joints
an gives the article A
a dab, or dab hand, is an expert

explanation.surface: A travelling specialist in illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; 'disorder' looks like an anagram signal but is the ailment itself. The definition is an adjective standing for someone always on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who flits from place to place in search of pleasure is a wanderer, which is what peripatetic describes.

clue.text: Worked near the console

indicators.note: worked means shaped or kneaded, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone working beside a games console or control desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked' signals an anagram of NEAR THE. 'console' looks like a noun, a control panel, but it is the verb meaning comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: To comfort or cheer someone up is to encourage them.

clue.text: Except for the Sabbath, chorister provides, insincere words

indicators.note: provides is read as produces or makes up out of, so the remaining letters are rearranged
except for means leaving out, so the letter is removed

parts.note: S is a standard abbreviation for Sabbath

explanation.surface: A choirboy, other than on Sundays, comes out with empty talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Except for' drops S (Sabbath) from CHORISTER, and 'provides' rearranges CHORITER. The anagram signal is a loose one.
explanation.definitionFit: Language meant to impress or persuade, often lacking substance, is grandiloquent speech.

clue.text: Serious attention given to home

parts.note: to give someone an ear is to give attention
a nest is a home

explanation.surface: Thoughtful attention is paid to the house.
explanation.definitionFit: Sincere and intensely solemn in manner is grave.

clue.text: Twig beneath a group of trees

parts.note: under means beneath
a stand is a group of growing trees

explanation.surface: A small branch lying below a clump of trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twig' is the informal verb meaning grasp, not a small branch.
explanation.definitionFit: To twig is British slang for to grasp or realise something.

clue.text: To some extent, a seed gets an advantage

indicators.note: To some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A tournament seed is given a head start.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the upper hand over a rival is being ahead or superior.

clue.text: Screen put up for instance to conceal stream

indicators.note: to conceal means to enclose, so one piece goes inside the other
in a down clue, put up means written upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: EG, short for exempli gratia, for instance
a rill is a small stream

explanation.surface: A barrier erected, say, to hide a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' gives GE, and 'to conceal' makes it wrap the stream, as a down entry reads upwards for the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A grating of bars over a window or opening is a protective screen.

clue.text: Toff takes a lover, an aristocrat

parts.note: a nob is British slang for a toff, an upper-class person
leman is an archaic word for a sweetheart or lover

explanation.surface: A posh man takes a mistress, as aristocrats do.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer or titled man is a member of the nobility.

clue.text: Convey in carriage, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken, giving a word that sounds alike

parts.note: mien is bearing or carriage, how one holds oneself

explanation.surface: Transport something in a horse-drawn coach, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carriage' looks like a vehicle but means deportment.
explanation.definitionFit: To signify or express a meaning is to convey it.

clue.text: Sort of specialists I trust completely

parts.note: ENT, ear, nose and throat, a branch of medicine
to rely on is to trust

explanation.surface: A patient declares full faith in a kind of medical expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Wholly or totally, with nothing left out.

clue.text: The Lizard — a horse I backed, accepting the tip you offered

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one piece goes inside the other
backed means going backwards, so the whole run is read in reverse

parts.note: a nag is an old horse
U is text shorthand for you

explanation.surface: A gambler on Cornwall's Lizard peninsula backs a horse on a tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses A NAG I to IGANA, and 'accepting' takes in U. The Lizard is a Cornish peninsula, a false lead; 'the tip' and 'offered' are surface padding around 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A large tropical American reptile is a kind of lizard.

clue.text: It's unfair to name retiring creature

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a cricket is a chirping insect

explanation.surface: Complaining that it's wrong to name a shy animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' reverses TO N to give NOT. 'Not cricket' is a British idiom for unsporting behaviour, from the game's code of fair play.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means unsporting, against the rules of fair play.
